strengths: The paper tackles an ambitious and challenging theoretical problem: policy regret minimization in partially observable Markov games against adaptive adversaries, bridging weakly revealing POMDP literature with adaptive game theory.

The proposed causal decomposition (Theorem 2.7) separating the world channel from the adversary aggregation operator in the observable operator model (OOM) framework is conceptually elegant and provides a clean foundation for handling partial observability and strategic adaptation simultaneously.

The decoupled formulation of the posterior-Lipschitz condition using a reference policy (Definition 2.2 and Assumption 2.3) successfully resolves the subtle circularity present in prior/concurrent formulations.

The analysis reveals an important insight regarding epoch schedules: geometrically growing epochs restrict the number of policy changes to O(log T), maintaining the policy transport cost at O(log T) and enabling an optimal O~(sqrt(T)) regret rate, whereas flat batching inevitably yields O~(T^{3/4}) regret.

The theoretical framework is thoroughly developed, featuring matching lower bounds (up to problem-dependent/log factors) and non-trivial extensions to unknown horizons and geometrically fading memory adversaries.
The paper is very well written, mathematically precise, and transparent about its technical choices and theoretical limitations.
weaknesses: The proposed algorithm relies on optimistic planning over confidence sets within POMGs, which is computationally intractable (PSPACE-hard even in known POMDPs). While standard for statistical sample complexity analyses under function approximation, it remains an oracle-based result without computationally efficient approximations.
The minimax lower bound (Theorem 4.1) establishes optimality with respect to T and the Eluder dimension d_E, but does not match the upper bound in terms of the horizon H or memory bound m.

The statistical regularity conditions (Assumption 3.1), particularly the bounded likelihood ratios (requiring lower bounds on trajectory probabilities) and the KL-to-operator error conversion, are somewhat strong and restrict the applicability to well-conditioned observation processes.
The paper is entirely theoretical with no empirical simulations, even on small tabular or synthetic toy problems that could illustrate the behavior of the epoch-based schedule.

strengths: Addresses an ambitious and technically demanding problem at the intersection of partially observable RL and game theory: policy regret minimization in POMGs against adaptive adversaries.

Identifies and elegantly resolves two key technical obstacles in existing/concurrent work: (1) eliminating circularity in the definition of posterior-Lipschitz adversaries via a fixed reference posterior-predictive measure, and (2) preventing the polynomial error accumulation of policy-transport costs by employing geometrically growing epochs ($T_e = 2^e$) rather than flat batching, thereby recovering the optimal $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ rate.

Establishes a principled causal decomposition (Theorem 2.7) separating the hidden-state world dynamics from the adversary's strategic response operators, allowing rigorous decoupling of MLE estimation from policy-dependent response analysis.
Provides solid extensions, including an adaptivity result to unknown horizons, an analysis of adversaries with geometrically fading memory, and explicit instantiations for tabular POMGs.
The manuscript is clearly written, logically structured, and provides thorough mathematical proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The proposed algorithm is an oracle-style statistical algorithm relying on optimistic planning over confidence sets of observable operators; as discussed in Section 5.4, this is computationally intractable (PSPACE-complete even for known POMDPs) in general environments.

The lower bound construction (Theorem 4.1) embeds a standard multi-armed bandit into a 2-step POMG with a trivial, non-adaptive adversary ($m=1, L=0$). While this captures the $\Omega(\sqrt{d_E T})$ dependency, it does not probe the minimax tightness with respect to horizon $H$, memory $m$, or the adversary smoothness parameter $L$.

Assumption 3.1(iii) imposes bounded log-likelihood ratios, which implicitly requires positive reachability / trajectory probability lower bounds (or explicit smoothing), a standard but non-negligible assumption in optimistic MLE frameworks.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging open problem: bounding policy regret in partially observable Markov games (POMGs) against strategic, memory-bounded adaptive adversaries.

The causal decomposition of observable operator models (Theorem 2.7) is technically elegant, rigorously separating the physical world channel (independent of policy and adversary response) from the adversary aggregation operator (independent of world dynamics).

Provides a clean resolution to the circularity issue found in prior posterior-Lipschitz adversary definitions by conditioning on a fixed reference policy measure, ensuring the model class and confidence sets are mathematically well-defined.

The geometrically increasing epoch design cleverly restricts the number of deployed policies to O(log T), which directly prevents the adversary policy-transport error from accumulating polynomially and preserves the minimax-optimal O~(sqrt(T)) regret rate.

The theoretical framework is thoroughly developed and well-rounded, featuring matching lower bounds with respect to T and aggregate Eluder dimension, tabular parameterizations, unknown-horizon adaptivity, and extensions to fading-memory opponents.
The paper is very well-written, mathematically meticulous, and clearly distinguishes between conceptual insights and detailed technical proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The algorithm relies on an optimistic planning oracle over POMG parameter confidence sets, which is computationally intractable (PSPACE-hard even in known finite-horizon POMDPs). The guarantees are purely statistical/information-theoretic.

Assumption 3.1 imposes relatively strong regularity conditions, such as uniformly bounded log-likelihood increments (requiring trajectory probabilities to be bounded away from zero via smoothing or strict positivity) and exact warm-up stationarity.

The lower bound in Section 4 is an embedding of a standard stochastic multi-armed bandit problem into a 2-step POMG, which confirms the tightness of the sqrt(T) and Eluder dimension scaling but leaves the optimal dependence on horizon H and memory m open.
The paper is entirely theoretical with no empirical simulations (even on toy or synthetic environments) comparing the geometric epoch schedule against standard flat batching.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental open challenge at the intersection of partially observable environments and multi-agent learning by establishing an optimal O~(sqrt(T)) policy regret guarantee against adaptive opponents in POMGs.

The proposed causal decomposition of observable operator models (Theorem 2.5) cleanly disentangles world dynamics from adversary response, enabling separate likelihood tracking and avoiding conflation between latent transitions and opponent adaptation.
The formulation of the reference posterior-predictive metric (Definition 2.2) elegantly resolves the subtle circularity present in prior posterior-Lipschitz definitions.

The epoch structure combining geometric caps with a statistical refutation test is well-motivated: Proposition D.5 proves that fixed-schedule batching provably fails (incurring linear regret under optimistic tie-breaking), and Lemma D.7 establishes that the number of early terminations is strictly controlled.

Comprehensive theoretical coverage, including matching lower bounds, horizon adaptivity, geometrically fading memory adversaries, tabular instantiations, and clarifying technical comparisons with concurrent work.
weaknesses: The algorithm is statistically efficient but computationally intractable, requiring global optimistic planning over confidence sets in POMGs (which is PSPACE-hard even in known POMDPs) as well as per-step MLE re-estimation during data collection.

The results rely on strong structural assumptions, including multi-step weak revealing (which introduces exponential scaling in the observation window kappa, |OA|^kappa |OB|^kappa) and strict trajectory positivity / bounded log-likelihood ratios (Assumption 3.1(c)).
Empirical experiments are restricted to small synthetic setups or low-dimensional discretized problems due to the computational hardness of the planning oracle.

strengths: Addresses an ambitious and fundamental theoretical question: establishing minimax-optimal policy regret in partially observable Markov games (POMGs) against adaptive adversaries.

Introduces an elegant causal decomposition of observable operator models (Theorem 2.5), which disentangles hidden-state world dynamics from the adversary's response function, enabling independent likelihood estimation.
Carefully resolves a circularity issue present in earlier formulations of posterior-Lipschitz adversaries by defining posterior-predictive policies with respect to a fixed reference measure.

Provides deep insight into the necessity of data-dependent epoch termination (Proposition D.5 and Lemma D.7), demonstrating that fixed rare-switching schedules fail catastrophically (incurring linear regret) under optimistic planning, whereas the proposed statistical refutation test achieves tight regret with controlled switching.
Comprehensive theoretical package: provides matching lower bounds, extensions to unknown horizons and geometrically fading memory, explicit tabular scalings, and validating experiments.
weaknesses: Like most optimistic MLE frameworks in POMDPs and POMGs (e.g., Liu et al., 2022a; 2023), the algorithm is statistically efficient but computationally intractable due to the PSPACE-hardness of POMDP/POMG planning and global optimization over the confidence set (though the authors honestly discuss this in Section 5.4).

Assumption 3.1(c) requires strictly positive trajectory probabilities (bounded log-likelihood ratios), which necessitates smoothing or discretization that can introduce large constant factors depending on the minimal reachability probabilities.

The complexity scales exponentially with the weak-revealing window parameter $\kappa$ via $(|O_A||O_B|)^\kappa$, which is standard for the weakly revealing setting but limits tractability when $\kappa$ is not very small.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and challenging problem at the intersection of partially observable environments and multi-agent reinforcement learning, establishing that $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ policy regret is achievable against adaptive, memory-bounded opponents in partially observable Markov games (POMGs).

Introduces an elegant causal decomposition of observable operator models (Theorem 2.5), decoupling the hidden-state transition dynamics (world channel $W$) from the adversary's response mapping (adversary aggregation $G$). This allows independent likelihood estimation and avoids operator entanglement.

Formulates a non-circular posterior-Lipschitz condition via a fixed reference measure $\mu^{\text{ref}}$ (Definition 2.2 and Assumption 2.3), fixing a technical circularity present in prior work where the Lipschitz metric itself depended on the candidate adversary response.

Uncovers a critical failure mode of fixed-schedule batching under optimism: Proposition D.5 proves that fixed epoch schedules can incur $\Omega(T)$ policy regret. The paper resolves this with a principled statistical termination test that ends misfitting epochs early while proving that policy switches remain bounded by $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ (Lemma D.7).
Provides a matching minimax lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{d_E T})$, together with natural theoretical extensions to horizon adaptivity, geometrically fading memory, and explicit tabular instantiations.

Complements the extensive theoretical development with focused empirical evaluations that isolate the failure of fixed schedules, confirm theoretical scaling laws, and demonstrate performance on a real-data classification task with an adaptive opponent.
weaknesses: The algorithm relies on an optimistic planning oracle over a confidence set in partially observable games ($\max_{(\pi, \xi) \in \Pi \times \mathcal{C}_{e-1}} V^\pi(\xi)$). Because POMDP planning is PSPACE-hard even with known transitions, Algorithm 1 is an information-theoretic / statistical benchmark rather than a computationally polynomial-time algorithm.

The early-termination test requires updating the maximum-likelihood estimate $\hat{\xi}_t$ after every data-collection episode. Although full optimistic planning is avoided within the epoch, per-step MLE re-estimation introduces a notable per-episode computational overhead.

The lower bound in Theorem 4.1 embeds a 2-step bandit problem with a trivial memoryless adversary ($H=2, m=1$). Consequently, while it confirms the minimax optimality with respect to $\sqrt{d_E T}$, it does not characterize the tight minimax dependencies on the horizon $H$ or adversary memory $m$.

Assumption 3.1(c) imposes bounded log-likelihood ratios (requiring all trajectory probabilities to be bounded away from zero, e.g., via smoothing), which can cause the constant $B_0$ to grow large when observation sequences are long or sparse.
